Mongolia is a country defined by its vast steppes and its nomadic civilization. For centuries, Mongolian herders have lived in harmony with the land. moving with the seasons and drawing on generations of traditional knowledge to manage their livestock, water and pasture under harsh and highly variable climatic conditions. Today, nomadic pastoralism remains an important source of livelihood for nearly one-third of Mongolia's population. Yet, range lands are much more than a source of livelihood for herders. Mongolia's steppes are among the world's few remaining temperate grassland ecosystems that retain much of their natural integrity. They sustain the migration of millions of Mongolian gazelles and provide habitat for globally threatened species, including the snow leopard, argali sheep, and Przewalski's horse. The interdependence between people, livestock, and nature has shaped Mongolian culture, identity, and way of life for thousands of years. But Mongolia's story is part of a much larger global rangeland story. From the savannas of Africa to the steppes of Central Asia and the pampas of South America, rangelands sustain the livelihoods of millions of people, support for food system and biodiversity, and strengthen climate resilience. They are also home to the cultures and traditional knowledge of peoples around the world. Yet, for too long, the true value of rangelands has not been adequately recognized in global policy, finance, and investment. When rangelands degrade, we lose much more than vegetation and fertile soil. We risk losing biodiversity, water retention capacity, carbon storage, pastoral livelihoods, and generations of traditional knowledge. Today, however, a new chapter is opening for the world's rangelands. With Mongolian initiative, the United Nations General Assembly designated 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists. This is much more than the celebration of a single year.
